strengths: Principled perspective connecting training-free diffusion guidance, stochastic optimal control (SOC), and posterior approximation errors via a surrogate variational upper bound.

The proposed Stein correction mechanism provides a clever particle-based mechanism to refine Tweedie-based posterior estimates on the clean manifold without requiring expensive simulation or backpropagation through full reverse SDE trajectories.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on molecular generation benchmarks (fa7, 5ht1b, and jak2 targets on ZINC250k), demonstrating substantial gains over the uncorrected training-free baseline and strong competitiveness with classifier-guided baselines like MOOD.

Insightful analysis of the out-of-distribution/off-manifold guidance failure mode, clearly demonstrating through sampling dynamics (Figures 5, 9, and 10) how Stein correction mitigates reward overestimation and gradient flattening.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation in Proposition 3.3 and Appendix B is somewhat informal: the surrogate value function gradient $\nabla_{x_t} \tilde{V}$ is decomposed via an ad-hoc concatenation operator $\oplus$ where the KL gradient w.r.t. $x_t$ is replaced by an SVGD update on clean space $M_T$ followed by re-noising. While algorithmically intuitive and practical, framing this heuristic mapping as an exact optimal control decomposition overstates theoretical rigor.

Lack of wall-clock time and computational complexity analysis. Evaluating the Stein discrepancy requires pairwise kernel computations among $N$ particles ($O(N^2)$) and extra forward passes through the score network at each reverse step. The paper lacks runtime benchmarks comparing SDG against standard guidance or SOC baselines.

Evaluation is limited to a single application domain (molecular graph generation with GDSS on ZINC250k). Given the general theoretical formulation of SDG for continuous SDEs, testing on standard continuous diffusion benchmarks (e.g., image guidance or toy continuous manifolds) would have significantly strengthened the claims of broad applicability.
Minor presentation and typesetting issues, such as the duplicate proposition numbering in Appendix B (Proposition 3.3 is labeled as 'Proposition 3.2' on page 14).

strengths: Principled motivation: The paper provides an insightful connection between stochastic optimal control (SOC), Tweedie-based posterior approximation in training-free diffusion guidance, and variational inference. Deriving the variational upper bound on the value function clearly illustrates why naive Tweedie approximations degrade.

Methodological originality: Introducing a Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) correction mechanism on the predicted clean manifold (MT) to refine the approximate posterior distribution—bypassing expensive Jacobian-vector products via a back-and-forth mapping trick—is an elegant formulation.

Compelling experimental gains: On molecular generation benchmarks across three protein targets (fa7, 5ht1b, jak2), SDG demonstrates substantial gains in novel hit ratio and docking scores compared to both uncorrected training-free guidance and classifier-guided baselines like MOOD.

Insightful diagnostic ablations: The analysis of sampling dynamics (Figure 5), reward overestimation, and molecule validity under varying low-density hyperparameters (Figure 6) effectively supports the claim that the Stein correction acts as a beneficial regularizer.
weaknesses: Mathematical and conceptual gaps in the control derivation: In Proposition 3.1, integrating a Dirac delta functional $\delta(s-t)$ over $[t, T]$ at the boundary $s=t$ is mathematically non-standard and requires careful formalization. Furthermore, in Proposition 3.3 and Equation (7), expressing the optimal controller $\tilde{u}^*(x, t)$ as a concatenation $\oplus$ conflates an algorithmic heuristic (discrete back-and-forth particle refinement) with a rigorous continuous-time control law.

Lack of runtime and computational complexity evaluation: The SVGD step requires pairwise kernel and gradient evaluations over the particle batch ($O(N^2)$ complexity) across node and edge features at each reverse diffusion step. The paper does not provide wall-clock time comparisons or memory overhead analyses against standard guidance methods.

Limited empirical breadth: Although molecular docking is a well-motivated application, the framework claims broad applicability to training-free guidance, yet it is evaluated exclusively on 2D graph generation with GDSS. Validating on continuous image inverse problems or 3D molecular conformation tasks would significantly substantiate the generality of the approach.
Minor presentation errors: In Appendix B (page 14), the proposition statement for the optimal controller decomposition is mistakenly labeled as 'Proposition 3.2' instead of 'Proposition 3.3'.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely problem: performing training-free guidance of diffusion models using off-the-shelf classifiers and reward functions, particularly when targeting rare, property-rich samples in low-density regions.

The intuition of using Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) as an interacting particle mechanism to refine Tweedie-based clean data estimates on the clean manifold before computing guidance gradients is creative.
The paper provides detailed visualizations of generated molecular structures and docking poses, alongside analyses of sampling dynamics across the sampling trajectory.
weaknesses: Fundamental theoretical and conceptual issues in the stochastic optimal control (SOC) derivation: (1) In Proposition 3.1 and Eq. (5), the marginal density is written as $p_t^u(x_t) = p_t^{1-\alpha(t)}(x_t) \exp(\beta(t)r(x_T))$, which is mathematically ill-defined since a marginal density at time $t$ cannot depend on an un-integrated terminal random variable $x_T$. (2) In Proposition 3.3 (Eq. 7 & Eq. 15), the paper claims that the optimal controller $\tilde{u}^*(x, t)$ decomposes as a Stein correction on $\mathcal{M}_T \oplus$ low-density guidance on $\mathcal{M}_t$, where $\oplus$ is defined as the 'concatenation of two consecutive steps'. In control theory and SDEs, a feedback controller $u(x, t)$ is an instantaneous vector field in the state space $\mathbb{R}^d$; it cannot be defined as an algorithmic concatenation of operations living on different manifolds. (3) There is a conceptual conflation between minimizing the variational bound $\tilde{V}$ over proposal distributions $q$ (variational inference to tighten the bound) and differentiating the value function with respect to $x_t$ to compute the drift control. SVGD operates on particles representing $q(x_T)$ in clean data space, not as a gradient field with respect to $x_t$.

Sign and derivation errors in Appendix B: In Eq. (17) and the preceding equations on page 15, the gradient of the log-transition kernel $\nabla_{x_T^j} \log p(x_t^j|x_T^j)$ is incorrectly written with an erroneous minus sign as $-\eta(t) \frac{x_t^j - \eta(t)x_T^j}{\gamma^2(t)}$, followed by replacing $\frac{z}{\gamma(t)}$ with $s_\theta(x_t^j)$ without the standard negative sign of score matching. Two opposing sign errors cancel out to reach the intended expression.

Flawed baseline comparison for the ablation study: The baseline 'SDG w/o Stein correction' sets $\alpha > 0$, actively steering the reverse process away from data density modes via $-\alpha(t) s_\theta(x_t)$. Pushing samples into low-density regions without regularization naturally causes off-manifold divergence and collapses validity/hits. Crucially, standard training-free guidance methods (e.g., DPS, Freedom) do not penalize density (i.e., they set $\alpha = 0$). The paper does not compare against standard training-free guidance ($\alpha = 0$), making the reported ablation misleading.

Limited empirical breadth and marginal performance improvements: (1) Experiments are conducted exclusively on molecular graph generation on ZINC250k with a single base model (GDSS). No standard continuous benchmark, image benchmark, or toy distributions are tested. (2) On the three evaluated protein targets, SDG only clearly outperforms MOOD on 5ht1b. On jak2, the novel hit ratio (9.367% vs. 9.200%) and top-5% docking score (-10.154 vs. -10.147) are virtually identical within error margins. On fa7, the non-diffusion baseline FREED achieves a higher hit ratio (1.107% vs. 1.011%) and a better docking score (-8.297 vs. -8.176).

Lack of runtime and computational complexity evaluation: A core motivation presented for avoiding simulation-based SOC is its computational cost. However, Algorithm 1 requires computing $N \times N$ kernel matrices and their gradients at each diffusion step, alongside multiple score evaluations on both $x_t$ and $x_T$ and backpropagating through Tweedie's formula. The manuscript provides no wall-clock time, latency, or memory consumption benchmarks comparing SDG to MOOD or standard diffusion sampling.

strengths: Relevant and challenging problem: addressing the bias and off-manifold drift of training-free diffusion guidance (e.g., Tweedie's formula) when sampling in low-density or out-of-distribution regions for scientific discovery.
Intuitive algorithmic idea: using particle-based Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) on terminal estimates to regularize guidance trajectories and enforce fidelity to the data manifold.
Extensive experimental effort in molecular generation across three protein targets (fa7, 5ht1b, jak2), supported by docking score distributions, validity metrics, and score norm dynamics.
weaknesses: Fundamental flaws in the Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC) formulation: In Equation 3, the running cost contains a Dirac delta functional $\delta(s-t)$ centered at the conditioning time $t$. In continuous-time SOC, cost functionals must be time-consistent for dynamic programming and Feynman-Kac representations to hold; defining a running cost that explicitly depends on the initial evaluation time $t$ breaks the Markovian structure. Furthermore, Proposition 3.1 writes the controlled marginal density as $p_t^u(x_t) = p_t^{1-\alpha(t)}(x_t)\exp(\beta(t)r(x_T))$, leaving the terminal variable $x_T$ unintegrated inside a marginal distribution at time $t < T$, which is mathematically invalid.

Severe discrepancy between theoretical propositions and the implemented algorithm: Proposition 3.4 defines the optimal control drift as the concatenation ($\oplus$) of the reward guidance and the Stein correction term. Because the state space is $\mathbb{R}^d$, the drift of the controlled SDE must reside in $\mathbb{R}^d$; concatenating two vectors would result in $\mathbb{R}^{2d}$, which is mathematically unsound. In practice, Algorithm 1 does not follow Proposition 3.4, but instead uses an ad-hoc pipeline (Tweedie projection $\to$ empirical SVGD step $\to$ forward re-noising $\to$ standard SDE step with a score-damping factor $(1-\alpha(t))$). The theoretical derivation does not rigorously support this multi-stage heuristic.

Unfair baseline comparison due to an un-ablated custom graph-order prior: In Appendix C.1 (Equation 27), the authors inject a domain-specific prior $p^\dagger(N_i)$ that strongly biases molecular size toward graph orders that have favorable docking scores in the training set. Baseline models (e.g., GDSS, MOOD, FREED) did not use this property-conditioned graph-size prior. The manuscript lacks an ablation isolating the contribution of this engineered prior from the proposed Stein correction, confounding the empirical claims in Table 2.

Heuristic derivations presented as formal lemmas: In Lemma 3.3, Equation 14 replaces an expectation over $p(x_T|x_t)$ with a single-sample Monte Carlo draw to equate the marginal score with the conditional score, which is a coarse heuristic rather than a rigorous mathematical approximation. In Corollary 3.5, setting $\epsilon(t)=0$ yields $x_t \leftarrow x_t + \gamma^2(t)s_\theta(x_t) + \gamma(t)z$, which uses the forward diffusion variance $\gamma(t)$ rather than a Langevin step size; equating this simple forward-reverse Tweedie reconstruction to an MCMC Langevin corrector is conceptually inaccurate.

Poor sample quality on image benchmarks: In Table 1, the CIFAR-10 experiments report extremely high FID scores (e.g., FID of 105.4 for label guidance, 70.0 for deblurring, and 68.9 for super-resolution). These values indicate severe degradation in image fidelity, undermining the claim of broad applicability across modalities.

strengths: The core idea of addressing the bias inherent in Tweedie-based posterior approximations for training-free diffusion guidance using Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) is novel and conceptually interesting.

The proposed 'back-and-forth' formulation is practical: by mapping particles to the clean data manifold $M_T$ via Tweedie's formula, applying Stein correction there, and re-noising back to $M_t$, the method avoids computationally prohibitive Jacobian-vector products through the score network.

The experimental evaluation on structure-based drug design benchmarks (fa7, 5ht1b, jak2) demonstrates solid results, outperforming or matching supervised classifier-guided baselines (such as MOOD) without requiring time-dependent classifier training.

The paper includes thoughtful diagnostic experiments, such as analyzing score norms, genuine vs. nominal reward dynamics, and structural validity across varying levels of out-of-distribution guidance.
weaknesses: Several mathematical formulations in Section 3 lack formal rigor: (i) In Equation (3) and Proposition 3.1, incorporating a Dirac delta $\delta(s-t)$ at the lower limit of integration $\int_t^T \dots ds$ is mathematically ill-posed; (ii) In Equation (10) of Proposition 3.1, the marginal density $p_t^u(x_t)$ is stated as $p_t^{1-\alpha(t)}(x_t) \exp(\beta(t)r(x_T))$, which inappropriately makes a marginal density at time $t$ depend on the random variable $x_T$ without integrating it out; (iii) In Proposition 3.4, the optimal controller is written using a concatenation operator $\oplus$ between two $d$-dimensional terms, which is mathematically invalid since the control $u^*(x_t, t)$ must belong to $\mathbb{R}^d$.

The gap between the surrogate stochastic optimal control theory and the actual algorithm is wide: Algorithm 1 executes an alternating heuristic (Tweedie mapping $\to$ SVGD update $\to$ re-noising $\to$ reverse diffusion step) rather than directly implementing the derived optimal control drift in Equation (4).

The empirical margin of the full Stein correction ($\\epsilon(t) > 0$) over the simpler Langevin correction baseline ($\\epsilon(t) = 0$, Corollary 3.5) in Table 2 is modest (e.g., Novel Hit Ratio of 9.167% vs. 8.722% on jak2, 22.690% vs. 21.722% on 5ht1b, and 1.156% vs. 0.956% on fa7). Given that SVGD incurs an $O(N^2)$ pairwise kernel computation across particles, the practical necessity of the repulsive Stein force over independent Langevin corrector steps is not conclusively demonstrated.

The image guidance results in Table 1 exhibit unusually poor FID values across all methods (e.g., FIDs between 70 and 172 on CIFAR-10 / AFHQ benchmarks), and the qualitative samples in Figures 15 and 16 show noticeable artifacts, suggesting that baseline configurations or hyperparameter choices in the vision experiments may be suboptimal.

strengths: The core intuition—that one-step Tweedie approximations used in training-free guidance deviate significantly from the true posterior and can be regularized via interacting particle methods (SVGD)—is conceptually interesting and relevant to the diffusion guidance community.

The empirical results on molecular generation tasks (Table 2) show noticeable improvements in Novel Hit Ratio over the uncorrected Tweedie baseline and competitive results against prior methods on several protein targets.
The paper provides an extensive ablation study exploring the impact of particle numbers, low-density schedules, and score dynamics during sampling.
weaknesses: Severe mathematical inconsistencies in theoretical formulations: In Proposition 3.1, the marginal density under the controlled measure is written as $p_t^u(x_t) = p_t^{1-\alpha(t)}(x_t) \exp(\beta(t)r(x_T))$. This is mathematically ill-posed because the left-hand side is a marginal density at time $t$, whereas the right-hand side depends on an unmarginalized, free random variable $x_T$ at terminal time $T$.

Artificial optimal control derivation and invalid concatenation operator: In Proposition 3.4, the optimal control $\bar{u}^*(x_t^i, t)$ is written using a concatenation operator $\oplus$ between a reverse drift vector and an SVGD update direction in data space $M_T$. A control vector $u \in \mathbb{R}^d$ cannot be the concatenation of two distinct $d$-dimensional operations. The back-and-forth particle update is an algorithmic heuristic, not a derived closed-form optimal controller of the surrogate SOC objective.

Trivialization of the low-density SOC formulation: The state cost in Equation 3 incorporates a Dirac delta $\alpha(s) \log p_s(x_s^u) \delta(s-t)$, which collapses the running cost into an instantaneous penalty at the current time $t$. This amounts simply to scaling down the unconditional score by $(1 - \alpha(t)) s_\theta(x_t)$ in the reverse drift (Algorithm 1, Line 8). Framing this standard temperature/score scaling heuristic as an SOC contribution is mathematically contrived.

Unfair baseline comparison via modified graph size prior: In Appendix C.1 (Equation 27), the authors introduce a specialized graph order prior $p^\dagger(N_i)$ that explicitly biases the sampling of molecule sizes towards those that achieved high docking scores in the training set. It is unclear whether baselines (such as MOOD and GDSS) were granted this same biased prior; if not, this introduces a significant confounding factor in the reported Novel Hit Ratios.

Overclaimed experimental gains: The text claims that SDG consistently surpasses baselines; however, in Table 2, SDG achieves a Novel Hit Ratio of 9.167% on jak2, which is lower than the MOOD baseline (9.200%), and on fa7, SDG (1.156%) is within standard error of FREED (1.107%).

Flawed and duplicate experimental figures: Figure 15 (Gaussian deblurring) and Figure 16 (Super-resolution) in Appendix E appear to display identical image grids. Furthermore, the reported image metrics in Table 1 show extremely degraded visual quality (FIDs between 68 and 105 on CIFAR-10), indicating that the guidance setup for vision benchmarks may be poorly tuned.
